'''John Charles Howorth Spence''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|ForMemRS]] [[HonFRMS]] (21 April 1946 – 28 June 2021) was Richard Snell [[Professor]] of [[Physics]] at [[Arizona State University]] and Director of Science at the [[National Science Foundation]] [[BioXFEL]] Science and Technology Center.<ref name=arizona/><ref name=googlescholar>{{GoogleScholar|UxmHb8sAAAAJ}}</ref><ref name=xfel>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150606173339/https://www.bioxfel.org/people/spence|archive-date=2015-06-06|url=https://www.bioxfel.org/people/spence|title=John Spence, Arizona State University, Department of Physics|publisher=bioxfel.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/nature09750| pmid = 21293373| title = Femtosecond X-ray protein nanocrystallography| journal = Nature| volume = 470| issue = 7332| pages = 73–7| year = 2011| last1 = Chapman | first1 = H. ==Education==
Spence was educated at the [[University of Melbourne]] where he was awarded a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in 1973 for work on double [[plasmon]] studies of metals under the supervision of [[Alan Spargo]].<ref name=spencephd>{{cite thesis |degree=PhD |first=John Charles Howorth|last=Spence |title=Double plasmon studies in several metals |publisher=University of Melbourne |date=1973 |url=http://trove.nla.gov.au/work/34613532|oclc=224889847}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1088/0022-3727/7/6/304| title = Determination of the single-scattering probability distribution from plural-scattering data| journal = Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics| volume = 7| issue = 6| page = 771| year = 1974| last1 = Johnson | first1 = D. W. | last2 = Spence | first2 = J. C. H. | bibcode = 1974JPhD....7..771J| s2cid = 250834812}}</ref> He conducted postdoctoral research at [[University of Oxford]] under [[Sir Peter Hirsch]], [[David Cockayne]] and [[Michael Whelan (scientist)|Michael Whelan]], and then at [[Arizona State University]] under [[John M. Cowley]], working alongside [[Sumio Iijima]], [[Ondrej Krivanek]] and [[David J. Smith (physicist)|David J. Smith]]. Later, he established his own group at [[Arizona State University]].

==Awards and honours==
Spence was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society|Foreign Member of the Royal Society (ForMemRS)]] in 2015. His nomination reads:<ref name=royal>{{cite web |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2015/john-spence/ |title = Professor John Spence ForMemRS |publisher=The Royal Society |archive-date=2015-05-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150502204524/https://royalsociety.org/people/fellowship/2015/john-spence/ |location=London}}</ref> {{centered pull quote|John Spence is distinguished for his innovative world-leading contributions to both [[biology]] and [[materials science]]. He co-led the team which conceived the first application of [[X-ray]] [[free-electron laser]]s (XFEL) to [[structural biology]] using protein nanocrystals and he pioneered [[femtosecond]] serial [[crystallography]]. He is also a world leader in the development and application of [[High-resolution transmission electron microscopy|atomic-resolution]] [[electron microscopy]] and its use for the study of atomic defects in crystals and semiconductors.  For example, he co-invented a widely used technique for locating impurity atoms in [[nanocrystals]], for directly and accurately imaging the chemical bonds between atoms, and published the first observation of [[dislocation]] kinks, at atomic resolution. He has developed new [[microscopy|microscopies]] and [[spectroscopy|spectroscopies]] which have given scientists new eyes to understand atomic processes in solids.}}

In 2017, he was made an [[Honorary Fellow of the Royal Microscopical Society]] (HonFRMS) for his contributions to microscopy.<ref name="RMS1">{{cite web|title=Current RMS Honorary Fellows|url=http://www.rms.org.uk/membership/honorary-fellows.html|website=www.rms.org.uk|access-date=18 December 2017}}</ref> Spence was a (corresponding) Fellow of the Australian Academy of Science, and the author of the book "Lightspeed"  (OUP 2019) on the history of attempts to measure the speed of light leading to Einstein's theories. For 2021 he was awarded the [[Gregori Aminoff Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.kva.se/en/pressrum/pressmeddelanden/aminoffpris-belonar-blixtsnabba-studier-av-makromolekyler |title=Gregori Aminoff Prize 2021 |access-date=20 September 2020 |archive-date=26 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220626203616/https://kva.se/en/pressrum/pressmeddelanden/aminoffpris-belonar-blixtsnabba-studier-av-makromolekyler }}</ref> He died in 2021.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.asu.edu/20210630-memoriam-regents-professor-john-spence|title = In memoriam: Regents Professor John Spence|date = 30 June 2021}}</ref>
